name: Medpor chin implant

card.summary: Hard porous polyethylene chin implant that tissue grows into; established chin option with little comparative trial data.
card.note: Tissue ingrowth makes removal harder than with smooth implants.

quick.overview:
Medpor is a high-density porous polyethylene used for chin implants. It is one of the three common synthetic chin materials, alongside silicone and ePTFE.

It is discussed in looksmaxxing as a hardmaxx way to add chin projection. Published evidence in the reviewed material is thin, mostly technique descriptions.
quick.mechanism: A shaped implant is placed over the chin bone; tissue grows into its pores, anchoring it and supporting blood supply [1].
quick.risks: General risks of chin implants include swelling, hematoma, temporary numbness, infection, displacement and nerve damage. Porous implants are described as harder to remove because tissue grows into them.

lead: A Medpor chin implant is a chin augmentation implant made of high-density porous polyethylene, a hard, slightly flexible material. It adds forward projection and sometimes height to the chin to balance the nose and jawline in profile, and is often done together with rhinoplasty.[1] Tissue grows into its pores, which anchors the implant and supports blood supply, but also makes it harder to remove than non-porous alternatives.[1]

It is one of several alloplastic (synthetic) options alongside silicone and expanded PTFE, with bone-moving sliding genioplasty as the surgical alternative.[1][2] In looksmaxxing it is categorised as a hardmaxxing option for chin projection.

A 2012 Aesthetic Surgery Journal paper describes Medpor as effective for chin augmentation and recommends reshaping its outer aspect, particularly in Asian patients, to create an appropriate chin shape.[2] A 2025 systematic review of seven single-center studies (1,126 patients) compared chin implants with osseous genioplasty and judged both effective.[3]

chain: Porous polyethylene implant placed on the front of the chin bone
Stronger profile and better balance with nose and jaw
angle.text: The implant physically adds projection to the chin, so the change shows immediately in profile once swelling settles, and tissue ingrowth holds it in place.[1]

paras: Commonly used chin implants are made of silicone, expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) or high-density porous polyethylene (Medpor).[2] Wikipedia describes silicone as soft and flexible and easy to remove but able to shift, ePTFE as flexible and strong and usually fixed with titanium screws, and porous polyethylene as firm with tissue ingrowth that anchors it.[1]

The 2012 paper notes that it can be difficult to contour the inner aspect of the implant to conform to the patient's mandible, and that without modification a gap may result; it recommends modifying the external aspect, particularly in Asian patients.[2]

In sliding genioplasty a segment of the chin bone is cut, moved forward or back and fixed with plates and screws.[1] The 2025 systematic review reported higher infection and dehiscence rates for implants (up to 23.8 percent in the studies included), transient neurosensory changes with genioplasty, and better soft-tissue predictability with genioplasty (85 percent versus 66 percent).[3] A 2024 review of facial implant materials noted porous polyethylene had low infection rates and that no material was shown to be definitively superior.[5]

Risks listed in Wikipedia include swelling, hematoma, temporary lip weakness or numbness, and less commonly infection, implant displacement, bone changes and nerve damage, with surgeon experience lowering risk.[1] A 2022 case report described chronic infection requiring implant removal after years, caused by an exposed tooth root.[4]

Evidence consists of descriptive papers and reviews rather than randomised trials. One paper describes a modified Medpor technique for Asian patients,[2] a 2025 systematic review compared implants with osseous genioplasty,[3] and a 2024 review of facial implant materials called for larger randomised trials.[5]
